item.title: Base Composition and Structure of Nucleic Acid Samples
item.stimulus:
A research team isolates nucleic acid from three different viruses. Some viruses carry DNA and others carry RNA as their genetic material, and the genetic material may be single-stranded or double-stranded. The team measures the percentage of each nitrogenous base in each sample. A dash (—) means the base was not detected.

Sample | %A | %T | %G | %C | %U
1 | 30 | 30 | 20 | 20 | —
2 | 25 | 33 | 24 | 18 | —
3 | 22 | — | 30 | 20 | 28

The team also studies a short segment of one DNA strand with the sequence 5′-ATGCCA-3′.
item.model_answer:
(a) Sample 3 is RNA. It contains uracil (28%) and no thymine. RNA contains the base uracil, while DNA contains thymine, so Samples 1 and 2 (which contain thymine) are DNA.

(b) In double-stranded DNA, C pairs with G and A pairs with T, so %C = %G = 18%. G + C = 36%, so A + T = 100% − 36% = 64%. Since %A = %T, adenine = 64% ÷ 2 = 32%.

(c) Sample 2 is not double-stranded; it is single-stranded DNA. In double-stranded DNA every A is hydrogen-bonded to a T and every C to a G, so %A would equal %T and %G would equal %C. In Sample 2, A is 25% but T is 33%, and G is 24% but C is 18%, so the bases are not paired in complementary strands.

(d) (i) The complementary strand is 5′-TGGCAT-3′ (aligned with the given strand it reads 3′-TACGGT-5′), because A pairs with T, G pairs with C, and the two strands run antiparallel.
(ii) A new nucleotide would be added to the 3′ end of the strand, which has a hydroxyl (–OH) group on the sugar; the new nucleotide forms a covalent bond there.
item.verification_python:
from fractions import Fraction
samples={1:{'A':30,'T':30,'G':20,'C':20,'U':0},2:{'A':25,'T':33,'G':24,'C':18,'U':0},3:{'A':22,'T':0,'G':30,'C':20,'U':28}}
for s in samples.values():
    assert sum(s.values())==100
rna=[k for k,v in samples.items() if v['U']>0 and v['T']==0]
assert rna==[3]
assert samples[1]['A']==samples[1]['T'] and samples[1]['G']==samples[1]['C']
assert samples[2]['A']!=samples[2]['T'] and samples[2]['G']!=samples[2]['C']
G=18;C=G;at=100-(G+C);assert at==64
A=Fraction(at,2);assert A==32
seq='ATGCCA'
comp={'A':'T','T':'A','G':'C','C':'G'}
aligned=''.join(comp[b] for b in seq)
assert aligned=='TACGGT'
assert aligned[::-1]=='TGGCAT'
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Base Composition and Strand Structure of Nucleic Acids
item.stimulus:
Students isolated three purified nucleic acid samples (1, 2 and 3) from different sources. For each sample they measured the percentage of each nitrogenous base. Samples 1 and 3 contain deoxyribose. The results are shown below.

Sample | Adenine (%) | Guanine (%) | Cytosine (%) | Thymine (%) | Uracil (%)
1 | 30 | 20 | 20 | 30 | 0
2 | 24 | 31 | 19 | 0 | 26
3 | 33 | 17 | 22 | 28 | 0
item.model_answer:
(a) Sample 2 is RNA. It contains 26% uracil and 0% thymine; uracil is found in RNA, while thymine is found in DNA.

(b) In double-stranded DNA the two antiparallel strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: every adenine pairs with a thymine and every cytosine pairs with a guanine. Therefore the amount of A must equal T and C must equal G, which is true for sample 1 (30% A = 30% T, 20% G = 20% C). In sample 3, A (33%) ≠ T (28%) and G (17%) ≠ C (22%), so the bases are not matched by a complementary strand, meaning sample 3 is single-stranded.

(c) C = G, so G = 18%. C + G = 36%. A + T = 100% − 36% = 64%. Since A = T, A = 64% ÷ 2 = 32% adenine.

(d) The complementary strand is 3′-TACGGT-5′, which written 5′ to 3′ is 5′-TGGCAT-3′. New nucleotides are added to the 3′ (hydroxyl) end of the growing strand.

item.title: Base Composition and Strand Structure of Nucleic Acids
item.stimulus:
A student is given three purified nucleic acid samples from different sources. Each sample was chemically broken down into its nucleotides, and the percentage of each nitrogenous base was measured. The results are shown below.

Sample | %A | %T | %G | %C | %U
1 | 30 | 30 | 20 | 20 | 0
2 | 26 | 0 | 31 | 19 | 24
3 | 22 | 35 | 18 | 25 | 0

The student also studies a short segment of one strand from Sample 1, which has the sequence 5′-ATGCCA-3′.
item.model_answer:
(a) Sample 2 is RNA. It contains 24% uracil and 0% thymine, and uracil is the base found in RNA in place of thymine.

(b) In double-stranded DNA, adenine on one strand pairs with thymine on the other, and cytosine pairs with guanine, through hydrogen bonds. Every A is matched by a T and every G by a C, so %A = %T and %G = %C. In Sample 3, A is 22% but T is 35%, and G is 18% but C is 25%. Because the bases are not matched, there is no complementary partner strand, so Sample 3 is single-stranded.

(c) G pairs with C, so C = 18%. G + C = 36%, leaving 100 − 36 = 64% for A + T. A pairs with T, so A = T = 64 ÷ 2 = 32%. Adenine is 32%.

(d) The pairing strand is 3′-TACGGT-5′, which is the same as 5′-TGGCAT-3′. DNA is an antiparallel double helix, so the two strands run in opposite 5′ to 3′ directions. The new strand's 3′ end therefore lies across from the given strand's 5′ end, and its 5′ end lies across from the given strand's 3′ end.

item.title: Base Composition and Pairing in Nucleic Acid Samples
item.stimulus:
A research team isolates purified nucleic acid from three different sources. For each sample, they measure the percentage of each nitrogenous base present. The results are shown below (a dash means the base was not detected; a question mark means the value was not recorded).

Sample | Adenine (%) | Guanine (%) | Cytosine (%) | Thymine (%) | Uracil (%)
1 | 30 | 20 | 20 | 30 | —
2 | 25 | 30 | 18 | — | 27
3 | 22 | ? | ? | ? | —

The team has independently confirmed that Sample 3 is double-stranded DNA. They also sequence a short region of one strand of Sample 1 and obtain 5′-AGTTCG-3′.
item.model_answer:
(a) Sample 2 is RNA. It contains uracil (27%) and no detectable thymine. Uracil is a base found in RNA, while thymine is found in DNA, so Sample 2 must be RNA.

(b) Because Sample 3 is double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C, so %T = %A = 22%. A + T = 22 + 22 = 44%. G + C = 100 − 44 = 56%. Since %G = %C, guanine = 56 ÷ 2 = 28%.

(c) In double-stranded DNA, each adenine on one strand is hydrogen-bonded to a thymine on the opposite, complementary strand, so for every A there is exactly one T and the percentages are equal. RNA is typically single-stranded, so there is no complementary partner strand pairing each adenine with a uracil; the amounts of A and U are therefore independent and need not be equal (25% versus 27%).

(d) The complementary strand is 5′-CGAACT-3′ (written in the other direction, 3′-TCAAGC-5′), running antiparallel to the original strand. During synthesis, new nucleotides are added to the 3′ end of the growing strand. That end has a hydroxyl (–OH) group on the sugar, which forms a covalent bond with the phosphate of the incoming nucleotide.

accurate: Criterion c1 treats Sample 1's double-stranded structure as established by the supplied information. Its equal base percentages are consistent with, but do not prove, double-stranded DNA. The pairing explanation is correct only conditionally.

solution: Parts (a), (b), and (d) agree with the rubric: Sample 2 is RNA; guanine in Sample 3 is (100 − 2 × 22) ÷ 2 = 28%; the complementary strand is 3′-TCAAGC-5′, equivalently 5′-CGAACT-3′; nucleotides are added at the sugar's free 3′ hydroxyl. For part (c), the independent solution correctly qualifies the intended explanation: Sample 1's composition does not establish double-strandedness, and Sample 2's unequal base percentages do not exclude partially paired RNA. Criterion c1 instead requires an unqualified structural explanation unsupported by the setup.
second.solve_issues: Part (c) implicitly assumes that Sample 1 is double-stranded, but only Sample 3 is independently confirmed to be double-stranded. Equal A/T and G/C percentages support, but do not establish, that Sample 1 is double-stranded; a single-stranded molecule could have those percentages by coincidence. Likewise, Sample 2’s composition does not establish that it is entirely single-stranded, because RNA can contain both paired and unpaired regions. The intended explanation for (c) is valid if Sample 1 is assumed to be double-stranded DNA and Sample 2 is assumed to be single-stranded RNA.
